notes.summary: An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning is different from the meaning of its words (a piece of cake = something very easy). SSC asks 1 to 2 idiom questions in Tier 1 and more in Tier 2. Most ask for the meaning of a given idiom; some put it in a sentence, some give a plain phrase and ask for the idiom, and a few test the exact wording. The literal meaning is almost always a wrong option.

concepts.title: How SSC asks idiom questions
concepts.body:
• Meaning of a given idiom: To take the bull by the horns. About 3 in 5 questions.
  • Idiom in a sentence: The boss will blow his top when he sees the mistake. The sentence helps you guess.
  • Plain words to idiom: Vennela made a big fuss about a small problem. Answer: a storm in a teacup.
  • Fill the blank or complete a dialogue with an idiom.
  • Correct wording: hit me below the hand → hit me below the belt.

concepts.title: A method that works
concepts.body:
1. Reject the literal option. Lie low is not about lying on a low bed; it means to try not to be noticed.
  2. Picture the image behind the idiom: sit on the fence, a person who will not get down on either side, so avoid taking sides.
  3. Use the sentence tone. If the sentence is about anger, the idiom means anger.
  4. Check the strength. Walk on air is very happy, not just content.
  5. Learn idioms in themes (anger, effort, secrets, money). Themed lists are easier to recall in the exam.

varieties.name: Meaning of a given idiom
varieties.how: Recall the figurative meaning. Strike out the option that takes the words literally, then the one that is too weak or too strong.

example.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To sit on the fence
steps: Picture someone sitting on a fence between two fields, not getting down on either side.
Options: take a high seat, avoid taking sides, place something on a barrier, occupy a bench next to a boundary.
Three options are literal; only one is figurative.

varieties.name: Meaning of an idiom in a sentence
varieties.how: Read the whole sentence; it usually tells you the mood (anger, relief, trouble). Pick the meaning that fits that mood.

example.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
The boss is going to blow his top when he discovers the blatant mistake in the balance sheet.
steps: A boss finding a blatant mistake: the mood is anger.
Options: attack fiercely, be very angry, dismiss from job, be very embarrassed.
Blow one's top = suddenly become very angry.

varieties.name: Idiom to replace plain words
varieties.how: Say the underlined words in one short idea (fuss, trouble, rarely), then pick the idiom with that meaning.

example.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the underlined segment.
Vennela made a big fuss about a small problem.
steps: Idea: too much fuss over something small.
Options: get a taste of your own medicine, barking up the wrong tree, add insult to injury, a storm in a teacup.
A storm in a teacup = great fuss over a small matter.

varieties.name: Idiom to fill a blank
varieties.how: Read the sentence around the blank for the clue word, then choose the idiom whose meaning and grammar fit.

example.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Kalam's house was within reach of the famous temple. It was just ______ from it.
steps: Clue: within reach, so a short distance.
Options: a stone's throw away, at one's fingertip, at arm's length, from pillar to post.
At arm's length means keeping someone distant, a different idea.

varieties.name: Correct wording of an idiom
varieties.how: Recognise the idiom and recall its fixed wording. Only one option matches it word for word.

example.q:
Select the idiom that can correctly replace the underlined part.
She really hit me below the hand by telling the boss about my mistake.
steps: The fixed idiom is hit below the belt (act unfairly).
Options: hit me the bricks, hit me below the books, hit me below the bottle, hit me below the belt.

varieties.name: Sentence using the idiom correctly
varieties.how: Fix the meaning of the idiom first, then test each sentence: does the idiom's meaning make sense there?

example.q: Select the sentence that uses the idiom a white elephant correctly.
steps: A white elephant = a costly possession that is of little use.
Option A: The new stadium, rarely used and costly to maintain, has become a white elephant. Fits.
Other options use it for a rare animal, a pale person or a lucky charm, which are literal or wrong senses.
example.answer: The new stadium, rarely used and costly to maintain, has become a white elephant.

tips: The literal option is almost always wrong; cross it out first.
Picture the image behind the idiom to guess its meaning.
In a sentence, the mood (anger, trouble, joy) points to the answer.
Learn idioms in themes: anger, effort, secrets, money, animals, body parts.
Revise the idiom flashcards daily; about 200 idioms cover most SSC questions.
For wording questions, trust the fixed form you have heard most often.
traps: Near meanings: at arm's length (keep distant) vs a stone's throw (very near).
Strength: walk on air means very happy, not just satisfied.
Bite the bullet (face something bravely) and bite the dust (fail) are different.
A slightly changed word (below the hand) makes the idiom wrong.
Not fit to hold a candle to means far inferior, not equal or superior.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A piece of cake
questions.solution: A piece of cake means a task that is very easy to do.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bold idiom.
Nobody knew about the surprise party until Rahul let the cat out of the bag.
questions.solution: Let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret by mistake. The context (surprise party) confirms it.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To hit the nail on the head
options: To say exactly the right thing
questions.solution: Hit the nail on the head = describe exactly what is causing a situation; to be precisely correct.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bold idiom.
With exams next week, Priya is burning the candle at both ends.
options: Exhausting herself by working too much
questions.solution: Burn the candle at both ends = overwork by staying up late and getting up early, wearing oneself out.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A red herring
questions.solution: A red herring is a clue or issue that draws attention away from the real question.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bold idiom.
The opposition's promises turned out to be a flash in the pan; nothing came of them.
options: A sudden success that does not last
questions.solution: A flash in the pan = something that looks impressive at first but quickly fails or fades. nothing came of them confirms it.
